SharedKnowledge.History: American Marine introduced the Grand Banks cruising-yacht concept in the 1960s. Early Heritage boats were built in Philippine mahogany; the principal transition to fiberglass occurred during 1973. Classic, Europa and Motor Yacht layouts must remain separate.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Traditional semi-displacement hulls with long keels and protected running gear; extensive teak interiors and, on many boats, teak exterior decks and trim. Construction and dimensions changed during long production runs.
OwnershipPriorities: Teak deck fasteners and moisture intrusion
Window and deck leaks
Steel fuel-tank corrosion
Exhaust and cooling systems
Legacy wiring and plumbing changes
Stabilizer and hydraulic-system condition where fitted
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Apply shared family intelligence only when the model generation and layout are affected; missing evidence remains unknown.

SharedKnowledge.History: Albin began in Sweden as a marine-engine manufacturer and developed compact fiberglass family cruisers such as the Per Brohäll-designed Albin 25. Albin Marine USA later developed American-market diesel cruisers, fishing boats and Taiwan-built trawlers. Swedish compact cruisers, American express/command-bridge models and Asian-built trawlers must not inherit one another’s construction assumptions.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: The Albin name spans materially different builders and eras: Swedish displacement cruisers, American-market solid-fiberglass and cored-deck family cruisers and express boats, and traditional Taiwan-built semi-displacement trawlers with extensive teak. Model and generation evidence is required before applying shared guidance.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm model identity and production era
Moisture in cored decks, pilothouses and window surrounds where applicable
Fuel-tank condition and access
Exhaust and raw-water cooling systems
Shaft, V-drive, rudder and prop-protection gear
Legacy wiring, plumbing, repowers and owner modifications
Exterior teak and underlying deck core on traditional trawlers
Parts support for original Swedish engines and obsolete equipment
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Treat Albin as several related product families rather than one uniform construction tradition. Apply shared ownership intelligence only to documented model generations; missing information reduces confidence and does not eliminate a candidate.

SharedKnowledge.History: Mainship emerged in the late 1970s with the economical 34 Diesel Cruiser and later produced several distinct American cruising families, including early single-diesel cruisers, Pilot-series Downeast boats and higher-volume performance trawlers. Model names and marketed lengths changed repeatedly, so identity must be tied to production years and hull family rather than the badge alone.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Mainship commonly used solid fiberglass hull structures with cored deck and superstructure areas, but construction details differ by model and era. The early 34 family, Pilot series and 350/390/400 trawlers must not automatically inherit one another’s structural assumptions.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm exact model, marketing name, year and hull family
Moisture around foredecks, windows, rails, flybridges and other cored structures
Fuel tanks, hoses and access
Exhaust risers and raw-water cooling systems
Shaft seals, alignment, rudders and protected-running-gear structures
Steering, bow-thruster and hydraulic equipment where fitted
Legacy wiring, plumbing, repowers and owner modifications
Engine-package suitability, access, noise and service history
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Apply family guidance only to documented model generations. Rebadged models such as the 350/390 and 400/41 Expedition/414 require year-specific identity checks; unknown information reduces confidence and does not eliminate a candidate.

SharedKnowledge.History: Vancouver naval architect and builder Bob Warman developed the original Camano in 1988. The shared 28-foot hull was marketed over time as the Camano 28, 30 and 31, while the Gnome designation identified the no-flybridge sistership. Tooling and production passed through several British Columbia owners; the design was later revived by Helmsman Trawlers. A separate Camano 41 appeared briefly for 2006–2007.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: The core 28/31 family uses Warman’s distinctive semi-displacement Keelform hull with a broad propeller-protecting keel and low engine placement. Published references describe cored hull sides and deck structures; exact laminates, tankage and equipment must be checked by year. The Camano 41 is a separate larger design and must not inherit 28/31 specifications.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm marketed model name against hull length and production year
Moisture around windows, deck hardware and cored penetrations
Fuel, water and holding tanks plus access and sender condition
Exhaust, raw-water cooling and engine installation history
Shaft, cutless bearing, alignment, rudder and steering gear
Plastic through-hulls and fittings where present
Bow-thruster, generator and electrical modifications where fitted
Flybridge ladder, helm controls, mast and bridge-clearance configuration
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Treat 28, 30 and 31 badges as year-dependent names for the same core hull unless evidence shows otherwise. Gnome means the no-flybridge sistership. Apply Camano 41 intelligence separately. Unsupported model identities remain in the database with low confidence rather than being deleted.

SharedKnowledge.History: Rosborough Boats began in Halifax in the mid-1950s under wooden-boat designer and builder James “Doug” Rosborough. His son James “Bob” Rosborough developed fiberglass prototypes in the early 1980s and delivered the first RF-246 in 1987. After roughly 25 years and almost 500 boats, the RF-246 molds transferred to Eastern Boats in Milton, New Hampshire, which continues the design.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: The RF-246 is a shallow-draft, trailerable, semi-displacement pilothouse hull rather than a conventional full-keel trawler. Current Eastern-built versions use a hand-laid hull, a one-piece stringer grid and foam flotation; the hull is described as solid fiberglass except for the transom. Legacy Rosborough-built boats were highly customizable and may differ in propulsion, structure, tankage and layout.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm builder era, exact layout and propulsion before comparing specifications
Inspect pilothouse windows, sliding doors, deck hardware and penetrations for leaks or core moisture
Inspect aluminum fuel tank, filler and vent hoses, filters and access
Inspect transom, outboard bracket or sterndrive transom assembly according to propulsion
Check cockpit scuppers, drainage and flotation-compartment access
Check hydraulic steering, trim tabs, wiring, shore power and owner modifications
Verify trailer capacity, brakes, tires, bearings and legal towing dimensions
For legacy diesels, inspect cooling, exhaust, sterndrive corrosion, bellows and parts support
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Treat RF-246 as one long-running hull family with major generation, propulsion and layout variation. Current Halifax, Yarmouth and Digby names identify interior layouts; Custom Wheelhouse is a documented factory configuration. Do not infer a diesel, shaft, shower or tankage package across the entire family. Unsupported RF-23 identities remain low-confidence placeholders.

SharedKnowledge.History: The production Monk 36 was designed by Ed Monk Jr. Production began in Taiwan in 1982, shifted to Nova Scotia in 1992 and continued through 2007. More than 250 hulls were built. The long production run and active Monk 36 Owners Association make it one of the best-documented classic cruising-trawler families.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Solid-fiberglass semi-displacement hull with full keel and protected propeller and rudder. Taiwan-built boats generally use more exterior teak. Nova Scotia-built boats reduced exterior teak and incorporated interior revisions, so construction and maintenance assumptions must remain generation-specific.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm Taiwan-built versus Nova Scotia-built generation and exact engine installation
Inspect deck, flybridge, rail and mast penetrations for moisture
Inspect windows, exterior teak and cabin-side leaks, especially on early boats
Inspect fuel tanks, fills, vents and accessible tank supports
Inspect exhaust risers, raw-water cooling, engine mounts and service history
Check shaft alignment, cutless bearing, stuffing box, rudder and steering gear
Audit shore power, charging, plumbing and owner-added equipment accumulated over decades
Verify mast-down and fixed air draft for intended routes
Use the owner association to confirm hull-number and year-specific differences
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Treat Monk 36 as one long-running product family with two major production eras. Do not generalize early exterior teak, bathtub-equipped aft heads, engine packages or later interior revisions across all years. Published 18,000 lb is a standard dry figure; equipped displacement can be materially higher.

SharedKnowledge.History: Willard Marine evolved from Bill Tighe and Willard Buchanan’s late-1950s boatbuilding work into a pioneer of production fiberglass trawler yachts. The William Garden-designed Vega 36 began in 1961. Hale Field-designed Vega 30 and Vega 40 families followed in the 1970s. Around 1975–1977 Willard replaced fiberglass-over-plywood deckhouses with molded cored-fiberglass superstructures on the later Willard 30 and 40 generations. Commercial and military work became dominant, and recreational-yacht production ended in the early 2000s.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: The early Vega families generally combined solid-fiberglass displacement hulls with fiberglass-over-plywood topsides or deckhouses. Later Willard 30 and Willard 40 generations used molded cored-fiberglass superstructures. This distinction is central to moisture inspection and must not be blurred across generations.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm exact hull family, variant, build year and HIN
Inspect plywood-backed early deckhouses or cored later superstructures for moisture
Inspect windows, rails, mast steps and deck penetrations
Inspect original black-iron or steel fuel tanks and access
Inspect exhaust, raw-water cooling and repower workmanship
Inspect shaft, cutless bearing, stuffing box, rudder and steering gear
Audit legacy AC/DC wiring, plumbing and owner modifications
Verify bridge clearance, rig handling and side-deck arrangement by variant
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Do not apply a generic Willard 30, 36 or 40 specification across variants or generations. Known differences eliminate incorrect assumptions; missing hull-specific data remains unknown and lowers confidence rather than excluding the boat.

SharedKnowledge.History: Halvorsen-associated Island Gypsy trawlers were built in Asia for international markets. The 32-foot family included Sedan, Europa and Fisherman configurations.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Solid fiberglass hulls with extensive teak interiors; many older examples have teak-over-fiberglass decks and teak-framed openings.

Inspect teak decks and deck cores
Inspect windows and exterior joinery
Inspect tanks and sanitation system
Inspect exhaust, raw-water cooling and shaft gear
Audit electrical upgrades
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Do not transfer accommodations or performance between Sedan, Europa and Fisherman variants.

Do not infer CHB specifications from similar appearance
Inspect teak decks, deckhouse and windows

SharedKnowledge.History: Cape Dory expanded beyond its sailboats into New England-style powerboats. The 30 Flybridge was produced in 1990–91; molds later went to Nauset Marine.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: The 30 Flybridge uses a modified-V fiberglass hull with balsa-cored hull sides and a full-length keel.

SharedKnowledge.History: Nordic Tugs was founded in 1979 around Lynn Senour's semi-displacement pleasure-tug concept. The 26 debuted in 1980, the 32 in 1985, and larger 37-, 42- and 52-foot boats followed; later naming and transom-platform changes produced the 34, 39 and 54 lineages.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Builder documentation describes stitched fiberglass reinforcement, vinylester resin, reinforced hull/deck and major-component bonds, tinned-copper wiring and stainless reinforcement at critical running-gear structures.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm model lineage and year-specific specifications
Inspect pilothouse and saloon window sealing
Check deck penetrations and core moisture
Inspect exhaust, cooling, shaft, rudder and steering systems
Inspect thrusters and owner-added electrical systems where fitted
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Pilothouse is standard architecture, not a separate variant. Treat 26, 32/34 and 37/39 as generation-sensitive lineages; never apply current-model specifications backward without hull-year evidence.

SharedKnowledge.History: Art Kadey and naval architect James S. Krogen founded the company around the Krogen 42, launched in 1977. The line expanded through the 38 Cutter, 36 Manatee, 54, 48 Whaleback, 48 North Sea, 39 and later 44 and current passagemakers.
SharedKnowledge.Construction: Early builder history describes heavy hand-laid fiberglass sandwich construction with closed-cell PVC foam core, teak joinery and commercial-trawler inspiration. Later models evolved to solid fiberglass below the waterline, Corecell in topsides and superstructure, protected propellers, reinforced collision structures and increasingly integrated systems.
OwnershipPriorities: Confirm exact model generation and hull-specific specifications
Inspect deck, cabin and window moisture pathways
Inspect fuel, water and holding tanks by age and material
Review exhaust, raw-water cooling, steering and running gear
Inspect stabilizers, paravanes, thrusters, hydraulics and generators where fitted
Audit decades of owner-added electrical and navigation equipment
SharedKnowledge.ResearchRule: Separate the coastal Manatee and sailing 38 Cutter from the Pure Full Displacement passagemaker line. Do not apply current 44 AE or 48 AE specifications backward to earlier 42 or 48 North Sea hulls.
